# Cloud execution mental model: AWS and transferable concepts

::: {.chapter-goals}
**By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:**

- explain how identity, object storage, containers, batch compute, networking,
  logs and billing cooperate in a cloud workflow;
- distinguish an AWS account, Region, Availability Zone, service and resource;
- explain why an S3 object is not simply a file on a shared POSIX filesystem;
- decide what belongs in a container image, an object store and a workflow work
  directory;
- map a Nextflow process onto AWS Batch and Fargate without memorizing a
  vendor diagram;
- identify security, scientific and cost assumptions that AI-generated cloud
  code cannot safely make for you;
- translate the AWS architecture to Azure or Google Cloud concepts; and
- run and completely remove a miniature, paid AWS experiment using synthetic
  data and a strict cost checklist.
:::

## Why a biologist should care

On an HPC cluster, an institution has already chosen the machines, network,
scheduler, storage and much of the security model. In a cloud account, your
team may be responsible for assembling those pieces—and every running or stored
resource can become a billable decision.

The cloud is not merely “someone else's computer.” It is an API-driven system
for creating computers, storage, networks, identities and managed services on
demand. That flexibility is valuable for burst capacity, collaboration and
repeatable deployment. It also creates new failure modes:

- a valid access key can still have dangerously broad permissions;
- a bucket can contain the right bytes but be in the wrong account or Region;
- a successful task can leave large intermediate files accumulating for
  months;
- a container tag can silently point to different software later;
- downloading data between Regions can cost money;
- a budget notification can arrive after spending has occurred; and
- technically correct infrastructure can violate consent, residency or
  institutional policy.

AI can draft infrastructure commands quickly. Your professional value is being
able to review the identity boundary, data movement, scientific inputs,
failure behavior, cleanup and evidence.

## Engineering objective

Build one coherent model of a cloud workflow:

```text
human or CI identity
        │ authenticated API requests
        ▼
workflow launcher ── submits jobs ──► managed batch scheduler
        │                                  │
        │ reads/writes state               │ starts isolated containers
        ▼                                  ▼
object storage ◄──────────────────── serverless or VM compute
 inputs / work / outputs                    │
        ▲                                   ▼
        └──────── logs and metrics ◄── logging service

container registry ── immutable image digest ──► compute
                                    billing ◄── every service used
```

This diagram has two kinds of traffic:

- the **control plane** creates, configures and schedules resources; and
- the **data plane** moves reads, references, containers, intermediates and
  results.

A pipeline can have correct control-plane configuration while reading the
wrong data. It can produce correct results while wasting money. Engineering
quality requires both planes plus scientific validation.

## Start with the vocabulary

| Concept | Meaning | Frequent beginner mistake |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud account | Administrative and billing boundary | Treating it as only a username |
| Region | Geographic service area such as `us-east-1` | Assuming every resource is global |
| Availability Zone | Isolated location within a Region | Treating it as another Region |
| Service | A capability such as S3, Batch or ECR | Thinking one service is one server |
| Resource | A created object such as a bucket or job queue | Forgetting resources persist until removed |
| API/CLI | Programmatic interface to the control plane | Assuming a command runs on the local machine |
| IAM principal | Human or workload identity making a request | Confusing identity with permission |
| Policy | Rules allowing or denying actions on resources | Using administrator access for convenience |
| Role | An assumable identity with temporary credentials | Embedding long-lived keys in code |
| ARN | AWS resource identifier | Treating a display name as globally unique |

AWS is the concrete example in this chapter. The mental model transfers; the
names and command syntax do not.

## Accounts, Regions and Availability Zones

An AWS **account** is a security, ownership and billing boundary. A company
usually separates production, development and security responsibilities across
multiple accounts rather than placing everything in one account.

A **Region** is where a regional service is operated. Choose it deliberately:

- is the service available there?
- may the data legally and contractually reside there?
- are the inputs already there?
- is compute capacity appropriate?
- what are that Region's prices and transfer boundaries?

An **Availability Zone** is an isolated location inside a Region. Batch
services can spread work across zones, but a single-zone filesystem or network
design can still create dependencies.

::: {.callout-important title="A Region is part of the analysis specification"}
Record the account alias or sanitized account ID, Region, storage locations,
image digest and workflow revision. “It ran on AWS” is not enough provenance.
:::

## Identity is the first dependency

Every cloud operation asks two questions:

1. **Who is making this request?** Authentication establishes an identity.
2. **May that identity perform this action on this resource?** Authorization
   evaluates policies.

These are different. A successfully authenticated identity can receive
`AccessDenied`, and that can be the correct security outcome.

### Human identities and workload identities

Humans should normally enter through organizational federation or IAM Identity
Center, use multi-factor authentication and obtain temporary credentials.
Compute should assume a workload role with only the permissions it needs.

Avoid:

- creating access keys for the AWS account root user;
- committing access keys, session tokens or credential files;
- placing credentials inside a container image;
- giving every pipeline `AdministratorAccess`; and
- sharing one person's credentials with automation.

AWS's [IAM best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)
recommend federation, temporary credentials, MFA and least privilege. The
[root-user guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html)
explicitly recommends minimizing root use and not creating root access keys.

### Least privilege is an iterative engineering process

A useful policy describes:

- actions: for example, read objects but not delete buckets;
- resources: the exact bucket prefix or job queue;
- conditions: perhaps the expected account, network path or encryption key;
- duration: temporary credentials rather than indefinite secrets.

Do not ask AI to “fix AccessDenied” and blindly apply the broader policy it
returns. First read the denied action and resource, then decide whether the
workflow should be allowed to perform it.

## Storage: S3 is not a shared directory

Amazon S3 is **object storage**. An object has bytes, a key and metadata inside
a bucket. A URI such as

```text
s3://example-bucket/project-a/sample-01/R1.fastq.gz
```

looks path-like, but `project-a/sample-01/` is a key prefix—not a POSIX
directory. Traditional assumptions may not apply:

- there is no normal `cd` into an S3 bucket;
- applications generally access objects through APIs or integrations;
- rename is commonly implemented as copy plus delete;
- request count and transfer can affect cost;
- permissions are evaluated by bucket, key, identity and sometimes encryption
  key; and
- placing an output object is not the same as atomically replacing a local
  file.

For a workflow, separate prefixes deliberately:

```text
s3://my-lab-bucket/inputs/     immutable test inputs
s3://my-lab-bucket/work/       recomputable workflow state
s3://my-lab-bucket/results/    retained deliverables
s3://my-lab-bucket/logs/       operational evidence, if configured
```

Use checksums or application-aware validation after transfers. A successful
upload proves that an API call completed, not that the correct biological file
was selected.

### Storage cost is more than gigabytes

The [S3 pricing model](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/) includes storage,
requests, retrieval for some classes and data transfer. Lifecycle rules can
expire recomputable work objects or transition retained data, but a deletion
policy is a scientific and governance decision—not merely a cost optimization.

## Containers and registries

A container image packages executables and runtime dependencies. A registry
stores and distributes those images. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR)
is AWS's managed registry.

Keep this boundary clear:

| Put in the image | Do not put in the image |
|---|---|
| tools and runtime libraries | patient or participant data |
| small stable configuration defaults | cloud credentials |
| entrypoint or helper scripts | large changing reference bundles by default |
| labels describing source/version | writable workflow outputs |

An image **tag** such as `:latest` is a movable label. An image **digest** such
as `sha256:...` identifies content. Use tags for human-friendly discovery and
record or deploy the digest for reproducibility.

Before trusting an image, ask:

- Who built it, from which source revision?
- Were dependencies pinned?
- What architecture does it support?
- Does it run as root?
- Is it scanned and patched under an explicit policy?
- Can the exact digest be recovered later?

## Compute: EC2, Fargate and AWS Batch are different layers

### EC2 virtual machines

EC2 provides virtual machines. You choose an instance family and size and are
responsible for more operational detail. It offers broad flexibility,
specialized hardware and Spot capacity, but also exposes more infrastructure.

### Fargate serverless container compute

AWS Fargate runs containers without you managing the underlying instances. You
request CPU, memory and related settings. AWS documents Linux Fargate billing
per second with a one-minute minimum; other charges such as public IPv4,
logging and transfer can still apply. Always check the current
[Fargate pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/fargate/pricing/) for the chosen
Region and architecture.

### AWS Batch orchestration

AWS Batch is a managed batch scheduler. Its core objects are:

- **job definition:** the execution blueprint—image, CPU, memory, command,
  roles and retry-related settings;
- **job queue:** where submitted jobs wait and how they are routed; and
- **compute environment:** where Batch can obtain compute, such as Fargate or
  managed EC2 capacity.

Batch schedules the work; Fargate or EC2 supplies the compute. Saying “the
pipeline runs on Batch” does not identify the compute model.

## Networking: the hidden architecture

A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is a logically isolated network. Subnets divide
its address space and are associated with Availability Zones. Route tables
decide where traffic can go. Security groups filter allowed traffic to and from
resources.

The words **public subnet** and **private subnet** do not themselves prove
security. Examine routes, addresses, endpoints, security groups and workload
behavior.

A container may need to reach:

- ECR to pull its image;
- S3 to read inputs and write work;
- CloudWatch Logs to send logs;
- external package or reference servers, if the design permits them.

Private workloads can use service endpoints for some AWS services. A NAT
gateway provides outbound internet access but can create hourly and
per-gigabyte charges. A miniature learning lab does not need a NAT gateway.

::: {.callout-warning title="Never copy a production network from a tutorial"}
Tutorial networking prioritizes comprehensibility and short-lived experiments.
Production biomedical systems require review by the organization's cloud,
security, privacy and compliance owners.
:::

## Logs, metrics and scientific evidence

CloudWatch can collect Batch job logs and operational metrics. Nextflow can
also produce a trace, report, timeline and DAG. These evidence types answer
different questions:

| Evidence | Question it helps answer |
|---|---|
| Batch job state | Did the cloud scheduler report success? |
| Container log | What did the application write to stdout/stderr? |
| Nextflow trace | Which process ran, for how long and with what status? |
| Object metadata/checksum | Were expected bytes stored or transferred? |
| FastQC/BAM metrics | Are the scientific outputs plausible? |
| Cloud billing data | What resource usage generated cost? |

No single green status proves all six.

## How Nextflow maps onto AWS

A common architecture has these roles:

```text
Nextflow launcher
  ├── reads workflow code and configuration
  ├── stages or references data in S3
  ├── submits each process as an AWS Batch job
  ├── records workflow state in an S3 work directory
  └── monitors job states and publishes outputs

AWS Batch job
  ├── receives CPU, memory, image and command
  ├── starts a container on Fargate or EC2
  ├── reads staged inputs
  ├── writes task outputs and logs
  └── exits with a status code
```

Nextflow's AWS integration is supplied by the
[`nf-amazon` plugin](https://registry.nextflow.io/plugins/nf-amazon/trends).
Exact configuration changes across Nextflow releases, so use the documentation
for the version you are running rather than copying an old blog post.

Conceptually, a cloud profile must decide at least:

```groovy
profiles {
    aws_batch {
        process.executor = 'awsbatch'
        process.queue = '<batch-job-queue>'
        process.container = '<registry>/<image>@sha256:<digest>'
        workDir = 's3://<bucket>/work'
    }
}
```

This is an architecture sketch, not a ready-to-run profile. Authentication,
Region, plugin/version requirements, IAM roles, networking, encryption,
resource labels and cleanup must be defined for the real environment.

::: {.callout-important title="Conda is not the cloud runtime plan"}
Nextflow documents that its Conda environment feature is not supported with
remote object-storage executors such as AWS Batch. Build the required tools
into an immutable container image instead of attempting to solve a Conda
environment independently inside every remote task.
:::

The launcher also matters. It may run on a laptop, a controlled virtual
machine, a CI runner or a managed orchestration product. It needs durable state,
network access and permission to submit and monitor jobs. Closing an unmanaged
laptop halfway through a production workflow is not a reliability design.

## HPC and cloud: translate, do not equate

| HPC idea | Typical AWS analogue | Important difference |
|---|---|---|
| User/project account | IAM principal and AWS account/project tags | Identity and billing boundaries are API policy objects |
| SLURM partition | Batch queue plus compute environment | Capacity can be dynamically provisioned |
| `sbatch` | Batch `SubmitJob` API | Submission requires cloud IAM and resource identifiers |
| Compute node | EC2 instance or Fargate task | Lifetime may be minutes rather than years |
| Shared project filesystem | S3, EFS or FSx depending on semantics | Object storage is not POSIX storage |
| Module | Usually software inside the container | Host modules are not portable to remote containers |
| `sacct` and job log | Batch state, CloudWatch and Nextflow trace | Evidence is distributed across services |
| Allocation limits | Quotas, budgets, policy and account controls | A budget alert is not a scheduler quota |

## The cloud bill is an output of the architecture

Think in components:

```text
total cost ≈ compute duration
           + stored bytes × retention
           + storage/API requests
           + data transfer
           + logs and metrics retained
           + networking resources
           + managed-service charges
```

Common surprises include idle virtual machines, unattached disks, old image
layers, S3 work prefixes, verbose logs, public IPv4 addresses, NAT gateways and
cross-Region transfer.

Treat each resource choice as a hypothesis. Start with a representative small
sample, read the trace and billing evidence, then revise CPU, memory and
parallelism. Cheapest per hour is not necessarily cheapest per completed
sample, and Spot capacity is not appropriate unless retries and interruption
behavior are understood.

## Biomedical data raises the stakes

The practical below uses synthetic text only. Before moving real human data,
answer these questions with institutional owners:

- Does consent permit this use and location?
- Is the account approved for the data classification?
- Are agreements such as a BAA required and in place?
- Which Regions are permitted?
- How are encryption keys governed?
- Who can read, copy, share and delete objects?
- Are access and administrative events logged for the required duration?
- What are retention, backup and deletion obligations?
- How are incidents and accidental disclosure handled?

Encryption is necessary but not sufficient. Encrypting a publicly accessible
or over-permissioned resource does not repair its authorization model.

## Transfer the model to other clouds

| Function | AWS | Azure | Google Cloud |
|---|---|---|---|
| Identity/policy | IAM roles and policies | Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC | Cloud IAM and service accounts |
| Object storage | S3 | Blob Storage | Cloud Storage |
| Container registry | ECR | Azure Container Registry | Artifact Registry |
| Managed batch | AWS Batch | Azure Batch | Google Cloud Batch |
| Logs/metrics | CloudWatch | Azure Monitor | Cloud Logging and Monitoring |
| Private network | VPC | Virtual Network | VPC |

This table maps responsibilities, not exact features. Nextflow has provider-
specific executors and plugins; verify current support, authentication and
storage semantics before translating a configuration.

## Review AI-generated cloud code

Before executing a generated command, Terraform module or Nextflow profile,
ask:

1. Which account and Region will this change?
2. Which identity will execute it, and where do credentials come from?
3. What new resources will persist and incur cost?
4. Are names, ARNs, subnets, roles and image architecture valid here?
5. Is any permission broader than the described workflow requires?
6. Can any input, log or error message expose sensitive information?
7. Is the container pinned by digest and compatible with the compute type?
8. Where are work files stored, encrypted and eventually deleted?
9. What does failure leave behind?
10. What commands verify success and complete cleanup?

If those answers are absent, the code is an unreviewed proposal.

## Practical 1: a zero-cost architecture review

This practical requires no cloud account.

Create `cloud-architecture-review.md` and analyze this proposal:

> Upload FASTQ files to a public S3 bucket. Put an AWS access key in the
> Dockerfile. Run Nextflow from a laptop using `:latest`, grant the job
> administrator access and keep the work directory forever in case it is
> needed.

Record at least one problem and one corrected decision under each heading:

```markdown
# Cloud architecture review

## Identity and secrets
## Data classification and access
## Container provenance
## Workflow launcher and recovery
## Compute and networking
## Storage lifecycle
## Cost controls
## Scientific validation
## Logging and audit evidence
## Cleanup and ownership
```

A defensible review should reject the public bucket and embedded credential;
separate human and workload roles; pin the image digest; place the launcher in
a durable managed context; define encrypted storage, retention and deletion;
and specify scientific and operational acceptance tests.

## Practical 2: miniature paid AWS lab

This optional practical creates real cloud resources and can incur charges. It
uses synthetic data and has two stages:

1. store and verify one tiny object in S3; and
2. run the official AWS Batch Fargate hello-world job.

AWS estimates its Fargate CLI tutorial at **less than USD $0.01 if resources
are removed promptly**, but that is not a guarantee of your total bill. Prices,
taxes, existing account resources, public IPv4 charges and Regions differ.
Check current pricing before starting. Set a personal ceiling such as **$5**
that you are genuinely willing to pay.

::: {.callout-warning title="Budget alerts are delayed, not hard caps"}
AWS states that budget information can be delayed and is updated only several
times per day. A $5 alert does not automatically prevent $6 of spending. The
controls in this lab are tiny inputs, no NAT gateway, short execution,
immediate teardown and verification.
:::

### Phase 0 — authorization and guardrails

Use a personal learning account only if you are authorized to create charges.
Do not use an employer account without approval. Secure the root user with MFA,
do not create root access keys and use a non-root federated or IAM identity for
normal work.

In **Billing and Cost Management → Budgets**, create a monthly cost budget. A
reasonable learning configuration is:

- budget amount: `$5 USD`;
- actual-cost alerts: `$1`, `$3` and `$5`;
- alert destination: an email address you actively monitor; and
- no assumption that the alert terminates resources.

Follow AWS's current
[cost-budget procedure](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/create-cost-budget.html).
Also inspect the account's current Cost Explorer/billing view so pre-existing
costs are not attributed to this lab.

Write down:

```text
spending ceiling accepted: yes/no
budget configured: yes/no
account contains other resources: yes/no/unknown
chosen Region:
start time:
```

Stop if the first two answers are not `yes`.

### Phase 1 — open CloudShell and prove identity

Open AWS CloudShell in the chosen Region. AWS provides CloudShell without an
additional CloudShell charge, although resources created from it are billable.
Its browser session supplies temporary credentials, so this exercise does not
need a local access key.

Set one Region and inspect the caller:

```bash
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="$AWS_REGION"

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws configure get region
```

Replace `us-east-1` if you intentionally selected another Region. Confirm that
the account and ARN are the learning identity you expected. Do not paste the
complete account ID into a public repository.

Create collision-resistant lab names from the current account:

```bash
LAB_ACCOUNT_ID="$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)"
LAB_SUFFIX="$(date -u +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)"
LAB_BUCKET="nf-biologist-${LAB_ACCOUNT_ID}-${LAB_SUFFIX}"

printf 'region=%s\nbucket=%s\n' "$AWS_REGION" "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  > cloud-lab-state.txt
```

`cloud-lab-state.txt` is your cleanup record. It contains an account-derived
bucket name, so keep it local rather than committing it.

### Phase 2 — create, verify and remove a tiny S3 object

Create a four-line synthetic FASTQ-like fixture:

```bash
printf '@synthetic-read-1\nACGTACGT\n+\nFFFFFFFF\n' > mini.fastq
sha256sum mini.fastq
```

Create the bucket. `us-east-1` has special bucket-creation syntax:

```bash
if [ "$AWS_REGION" = "us-east-1" ]; then
  aws s3api create-bucket --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --region "$AWS_REGION"
else
  aws s3api create-bucket \
    --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
    --region "$AWS_REGION" \
    --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$AWS_REGION"
fi
```

Block public access explicitly:

```bash
aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  'BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true'
```

Upload, list and download the object:

```bash
aws s3 cp mini.fastq "s3://${LAB_BUCKET}/inputs/mini.fastq"
aws s3 ls "s3://${LAB_BUCKET}/inputs/"
aws s3 cp "s3://${LAB_BUCKET}/inputs/mini.fastq" mini.downloaded.fastq
```

Compare the bytes:

```bash
sha256sum mini.fastq mini.downloaded.fastq
cmp mini.fastq mini.downloaded.fastq
echo "cmp_exit_code=$?"
```

An exit code of `0` and matching hashes prove byte identity. They do not prove
that a real FASTQ has valid pairing, read counts or biological provenance.

Inspect the controls rather than assuming them:

```bash
aws s3api get-bucket-location --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET"
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET"
aws s3api head-object --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --key inputs/mini.fastq
```

Now remove only the known object, verify the bucket is empty, then remove it:

```bash
aws s3api delete-object \
  --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  --key inputs/mini.fastq

aws s3api list-objects-v2 \
  --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" \
  --query 'Contents[].Key'

aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET" --region "$AWS_REGION"
```

The list should return no keys before `delete-bucket`. Verify deletion:

```bash
aws s3api head-bucket --bucket "$LAB_BUCKET"
echo "expected_nonzero_after_deletion=$?"
```

The final call should fail because the bucket no longer exists or is no longer
accessible. This is an intentional negative test.

### Phase 3 — run one tiny AWS Batch Fargate job

Use AWS's maintained
[AWS Batch Fargate CLI tutorial](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/userguide/getting-started-with-fargate-using-the-aws-cli.html),
not a copied third-party command sequence. It takes approximately 15–20
minutes and walks through:

1. creating the Batch task execution role;
2. creating a Fargate compute environment;
3. creating a job queue;
4. registering a small job definition;
5. submitting and monitoring one job;
6. reading its CloudWatch log; and
7. disabling and deleting the queue and compute environment and removing the
   remaining tutorial resources.

Before executing each tutorial command, replace its names with a clear prefix
such as `nf-biologist-lab-` and check that `AWS_REGION` is still correct:

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity
printf 'Region: %s\n' "$AWS_REGION"
```

Do not add a NAT gateway, large data, GPUs or a long-running service. Choose
Fargate and use the tutorial's stated CPU, memory and single short hello-world
command. Fargate accepts only specific CPU/memory combinations; do not enlarge
the request merely because more capacity sounds safer.

Capture this evidence in `cloud-batch-evidence.txt`:

```text
Region:
job name:
job ID:
final Batch status:
container image/tag or digest:
requested vCPU and memory:
CloudWatch log group/stream:
first and last log timestamps:
job output summary:
cleanup completion time:
```

Do not publish raw account IDs, ARNs or logs until you have reviewed them.

### Phase 4 — prove cleanup

Follow the tutorial cleanup in dependency order. Batch generally requires a
queue or compute environment to be disabled before it can be deleted. Wait for
the reported state instead of repeatedly issuing deletion commands.

Then inspect, rather than assume:

```bash
aws batch describe-job-queues
aws batch describe-compute-environments
aws batch describe-job-definitions --status ACTIVE
aws s3api list-buckets --query 'Buckets[].Name'
```

Filter the output for your `nf-biologist-lab-` prefix. Confirm that no lab
queue, compute environment, active job definition or bucket remains. Review
the IAM role and CloudWatch log group created by the tutorial and remove them
if the tutorial's cleanup did not do so. Do not delete unrelated resources.

Record:

```text
lab bucket absent: yes/no
lab queue absent: yes/no
lab compute environment absent: yes/no
lab job definition inactive/removed: yes/no
lab IAM role removed: yes/no
lab log group retained or removed intentionally:
end time:
```

Check the billing dashboard later because cost data is delayed. The goal is not
to claim a universal exact price; it is to connect each observed charge to a
resource and prove that no billable lab resource was left running.

### Optional extension — understand ECR without retaining an image

If you already understand Docker and want to practice the registry layer,
follow the official
[ECR getting-started procedure](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/getting-started-cli.html)
with a tiny image. Record both tag and digest, pull by digest, then delete the
image and repository immediately. Review current ECR storage and transfer
pricing first. This extension is intentionally optional because Chapter 9
teaches image construction in depth.

## Practical acceptance checklist

The paid lab is complete only when you can show:

- expected identity and Region were checked before resource creation;
- a budget and personal spending ceiling were established;
- only synthetic data was uploaded;
- public S3 access was blocked;
- upload/download bytes matched;
- the Batch job reached `SUCCEEDED` and its log was inspected;
- requested CPU, memory and image were recorded;
- every lab resource was enumerated after teardown; and
- delayed billing was checked later.

## Hands-on exercise: design the next experiment

Design—but do not deploy—a cloud version of this book's five-process pipeline:
raw FastQC, Trim Galore, trimmed FastQC, Bowtie2 alignment/sort and BAM QC.

In `cloud-nextflow-design.md`, provide:

1. a diagram showing launcher, S3 prefixes, Batch, compute, registry and logs;
2. separate human, launcher and task identities;
3. proposed Region and the evidence needed to approve it;
4. input, work and result retention rules;
5. an immutable image reference strategy;
6. CPU and memory hypotheses for each process;
7. failure, retry and `-resume` behavior;
8. operational and scientific acceptance tests;
9. a cost model listing every potentially billable component; and
10. a teardown or production-ownership plan.

Then ask an AI system to review the design. Add a section titled **AI claims I
verified**. For every accepted suggestion, identify the authoritative provider
or Nextflow documentation, version and date checked. Reject suggestions that
assume permissions, compliance approval or prices without evidence.

## Ten interview questions

### 1. What is the difference between AWS Batch and Fargate?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

AWS Batch is the scheduling/orchestration layer: it accepts jobs, evaluates
queues and places work. Fargate is one compute option that supplies serverless
container capacity. Batch can also use managed EC2 capacity. A complete answer
names both layers because they affect cost, capability and operations
differently.

</details>

### 2. Why is an S3 prefix not a normal directory?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

S3 stores objects identified by bucket and key. Slash-separated prefixes give
keys a hierarchical appearance, but there is no POSIX directory tree with the
same rename, locking, permissions and random-access semantics. Applications
must use an object API or an integration that deliberately translates those
semantics.

</details>

### 3. A Batch job says `SUCCEEDED`. Is the analysis valid?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

No. It means the scheduled command reported successful completion. I would
also verify input identity and checksums, workflow revision, image digest,
parameters, expected outputs and domain metrics such as read counts, FastQC,
mapping statistics and sample identity.

</details>

### 4. Why should a workload use an IAM role instead of an access key in its image?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

A role provides temporary, rotatable credentials to the workload and can be
scoped with least-privilege policies. A key baked into an image is long-lived,
can be copied with every image pull, is difficult to rotate and turns the image
registry into a credential exposure path.

</details>

### 5. Why does a budget alert not guarantee a spending cap?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

Billing data and budget evaluation are delayed, and an alert is ordinarily a
notification rather than an immediate resource kill switch. Cost control also
requires quotas and policy where appropriate, small initial tests, bounded
resources, ownership, monitoring and explicit teardown.

</details>

### 6. Why pin a container digest if the image already has a version tag?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

A registry tag is a reference that can be moved to different content. A digest
is content-addressed and identifies the exact image manifest. I can retain a
readable version tag for discovery while recording or executing the digest for
reproducibility.

</details>

### 7. What belongs in the Nextflow S3 work directory, and why does lifecycle matter?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

The work directory contains staged task inputs, commands, metadata and outputs
used for execution and resume. It can grow much larger than final results.
Deleting it too early breaks resume and audit needs; retaining it indefinitely
creates cost and governance problems. Retention must reflect recovery,
reproducibility, policy and whether the data can be recomputed.

</details>

### 8. How would you investigate `AccessDenied` safely?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

I would identify the caller, denied API action, exact resource and relevant
identity/resource/key policies. I would decide whether the action is actually
required, then grant the narrowest justified permission and retest. I would
not attach administrator access merely to make the error disappear.

</details>

### 9. Why can data transfer dominate an apparently cheap compute design?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

Genomics inputs and intermediates are large. Repeated downloads, cross-Region
movement, internet egress or traffic through charged networking components can
outweigh a short compute task. I place compute near approved data, minimize
unnecessary copies and model storage requests and transfer explicitly.

</details>

### 10. What must you verify before moving human genomic data to a cloud account?

<details><summary>Model answer</summary>

I need institutional approval and evidence for consented use, data
classification, contracts, permitted account and Region, identity and least
privilege, encryption/key governance, networking, logging, retention, backup,
deletion and incident response. Technical encryption alone does not establish
legal or organizational authorization.

</details>

## What you should now be able to explain

You should be able to narrate a cloud workflow from authenticated submission
through object access, container resolution, scheduling, execution, logging,
scientific validation, billing and cleanup. More importantly, you should be
able to stop an unsafe deployment and name the missing evidence.

The next chapter introduces Git: the system that records changes to the
workflow, infrastructure, documentation and evidence you have learned to
reason about.
